scenes.title: Taxpayer Absorbed Risk
scenes.narration_text:
It's lobbied outcome.

Drug companies love the N.I.H. Taxpayers absorb the risk of basic research; industry patents whatever works.
scenes.context: Describing the relationship between public funding of risky research and private patenting of results.

scenes.title: The Kitchen Analogy
scenes.narration_text:

But independent trials

scenes.narration_text: When Congress created the Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute, or PCORI, in twenty ten, industry successfully lobbied to prohibit it

scenes.context: Legislative restrictions were put in place to ensure drug prices wouldn't be threatened by new research.

scenes.title: The Revolving Door
scenes.narration_text: They wrote it down. In legislation. On purpose. The revolving door helps. N.I.H. advisory committees include industry representatives.
scenes.context: The narrator describes the systemic way industry and the NIH are intertwined.

scenes.title: Misaligned Incentives
scenes.narration_text: Former N.I.H. officials join pharmaceutical boards. Academic researchers depend on industry grants. Everyone's incentives align against cheap,

scenes.narration_text: the same terrible outcome, purely by coincidence, repeatedly, for decades. Basic research produces publications. Publications produce tenure.
scenes.context: The focus on academic advancement through papers rather than patient outcomes is highlighted.

scenes.title: Need for Papers
scenes.narration_text: Tenure produces more grants. Nobody in this cycle needs anyone to get better. They need papers. The three point three percent allocation isn't a mystery.
scenes.context: Narrator emphasizes that the medical research system prioritizes data and grants over actual healing.

scenes.narration_text: It's a business model. The Efficiency Gap: A Tale of Two Trials. The difference between efficient and inefficient trial design isn't theoretical.
scenes.context: Transitioning to a real-world comparison of trial designs during the COVID-19 pandemic.

scenes.narration_text: Humanity accidentally ran a controlled experiment on itself during COVID. Two countries. Same disease. One spent like it was trying to cure death.
scenes.context: Setting the stage for the comparison between the US and UK approaches to COVID trials.

scenes.title: Dinner vs SUV
scenes.narration_text: The British cured disease for the price of a nice dinner per patient. America spent the price of a luxury SUV per patient and cured nothing.
scenes.context: A stark visual comparison of the spending habits of the two nations' medical research departments.

scenes.title: Capability vs Addiction
scenes.narration_text: The problem isn't that curing disease is hard. The N.I.H. doesn't have a capability problem. It has a shopping addiction.
scenes.context: The narrator argues the issue is spending habits, not a lack of scientific ability.

scenes.title: Budget Misallocation
scenes.narration_text: The Death Toll: Opportunity Cost of Misallocation. When you misallocate the vast majority of a forty-seven billion dollar annual budget into
scenes.context: Introducing the lethal consequences of wasting the NIH budget on inefficient research.

scenes.title: Composting People
scenes.narration_text: low-efficiency research instead of high-efficiency clinical trials, you aren't just wasting money. You are composting people.
scenes.context: A metaphorical description of the human lives lost due to bureaucratic waste.

scenes.title: Cost Per QALY
scenes.narration_text: Cost Per Q.A.L.Y. (Quality-Adjusted Life Year). Standard N.I.H. Portfolio: fifty thousand dollars per Q.A.L.Y. at standard medical research R.O.I.
scenes.context: Technical comparison of the ROI of standard NIH research using the QALY metric.

scenes.title: ROI Comparison

scenes.narration_text: cost thirty times less than traditional R.C.T.s (fourteen million dollars versus four hundred and twenty million dollars). Same science.
scenes.context: Showing that the science is identical, but the price tag is dramatically different.

scenes.title: Death Equivalent Intro
scenes.narration_text: Fewer catered meetings. The "Death Equivalent" of Budget Misallocation. The annual opportunity cost is approximately one hundred million
scenes.context: Calculating the total human cost of not using more efficient trial methods.

scenes.narration_text: quality-adjusted life years, or Q.A.L.Y.s, and about seven million death-equivalents per year.
scenes.context: Providing a staggering statistic of potential lives lost due to budget mismanagement.

scenes.title: Conservative Death Estimate
scenes.narration_text: Even the most conservative estimate is approximately ten million Q.A.L.Y.s and seven hundred thousand preventable deaths annually.
scenes.context: The narrator concludes with the most cautious, yet still tragic, estimate of annual preventable deaths.

scenes.title: NIH Cost Disparity
scenes.narration_text: For every dollar spent on pragmatic trials producing Q.A.L.Y.s, the N.I.H. spends twelve thousand five hundred dollars to achieve the same result.
scenes.context: Comparing the cost efficiency of pragmatic trials versus standard NIH spending.

scenes.title: Potential Capacity
scenes.narration_text: You are operating at zero point zero zero eight percent of your potential capacity to save lives.
scenes.context: Highlighting the massive inefficiency in current life-saving potential.

scenes.title: Car Efficiency Analogy
scenes.narration_text: If your car ran at zero point zero zero eight percent efficiency, it would move one inch per gallon.
scenes.context: An analogy comparing medical research efficiency to a car's fuel economy.

scenes.title: Heart Function Analogy
scenes.narration_text: If your heart pumped at zero point zero zero eight percent efficiency, you'd be dead before finishing this sentence.
scenes.context: An analogy comparing research efficiency to a failing human heart.

scenes.title: Rewarding Inefficiency
scenes.narration_text: Your medical research system runs at zero point zero zero eight percent efficiency, and you gave it a raise.
scenes.context: Criticizing the decision to increase funding for an inefficient system.

scenes.title: The Translation Crisis
scenes.narration_text:
The Translation Crisis: All Theory, No Medicine.

The problem is not a shortage of ideas. It is a shortage of anyone bothering to test them.
scenes.context: Defining the 'Translation Crisis' as a lack of clinical testing rather than ideas.

scenes.title: Safe Human Drugs
scenes.narration_text: There are over twenty thousand F.D.A. approved drugs known to be safe in humans. There are between forty-seven hundred

scenes.title: Repurposable Compounds
scenes.narration_text: and sixty-eight hundred repurposable compounds, which are clinically-tested candidates (including three thousand four hundred

scenes.narration_text:
and twenty-two marketed drugs) gathering dust.

scenes.context: Highlighting the surplus of untested dementia treatment ideas that are currently ignored.

scenes.narration_text: The number of clinical trials available for your grandma in Saint Louis is zero. You have a warehouse of safe molecules
scenes.context: The lack of actual clinical trials available for patients in need despite the surplus of drugs.

scenes.title: Testing Facility Closed
scenes.narration_text: that have never been systematically tested for new uses. The warehouse is full. The testing facility is closed for a team-building retreat.
scenes.context: An analogy for the lack of systematic testing despite available molecules.

scenes.title: Publishing House Metric
scenes.narration_text: The N.I.H. is, by its own metrics, a publishing house that occasionally dabbles in medicine:
scenes.context: Characterizing the NIH as more of a publisher than a medical institution.

scenes.title: Paper Production
scenes.narration_text: Two point five million N.I.H. funded papers are published annually. About fifty new treatments are approved annually.
scenes.context: The massive volume of NIH-funded papers compared to the tiny number of actual treatments.

scenes.title: Conversion Failure
scenes.narration_text: The conversion rate from paper to patient is zero point zero zero two percent. For every fifty thousand papers, one drug reaches a human.
scenes.context: The extremely low success rate of turning academic papers into approved drugs.

scenes.title: Citation Loop
scenes.narration_text: The rest become citations in other papers, which become citations in other papers, in an infinite loop of academics reading each other's homework.
scenes.context: Describing the self-referential nature of academic publishing.

scenes.title: Low Participation
scenes.narration_text:
Plenty of Knowledge. No Translation.

About five percent of patients have participated in trials.
scenes.context: Statistics on the small number of patients currently participating in clinical trials.

scenes.title: Invitation Gap
scenes.narration_text: About fifty percent of patients are willing to participate if invited. Only nine to eleven percent of patients are actually invited.
scenes.context: The massive gap between patient willingness and the actual invitations to join trials.

scenes.title: Asking the Question
scenes.narration_text: Half of all patients would join a clinical trial if asked. Almost nobody asks. It's like having a room full of volunteers and a clipboard,
scenes.context: Most patients would join trials if they were simply asked, but the system focuses on theory.

scenes.title: Understanding vs Curing
scenes.narration_text:
and choosing to study the clipboard.

Understanding disease and curing disease are completely different activities.
scenes.context: Distinguishing between the academic study of disease and its actual clinical cure.

scenes.title: Microscope Choice
scenes.narration_text: One requires microscopes. The other requires giving people medicine and seeing if they stop dying. The N.I.H. chose microscopes.
scenes.context: The NIH's institutional preference for microscopic study over direct clinical application.

scenes.title: The Club Goods Scam
scenes.narration_text:
The Public Goods versus Club Goods Scam.

The N.I.H. claims to produce "public goods" like open science and training.
scenes.context: Introducing the argument that NIH research serves private industry interests over public benefit.

scenes.title: Pharma Subsidy
scenes.narration_text: What it actually produces is a free R. and D. department for pharmaceutical companies, funded by the same people who then pay full price for the drugs.
scenes.context: Explaining how taxpayers fund research that private drug companies then profit from.

scenes.title: Taxpayer Funded Research
scenes.narration_text: Taxpayers funded research behind ninety-nine percent of new drugs (three hundred and fifty-six drugs, twenty ten to twenty nineteen).
scenes.context: Statistics showing that nearly all new drugs are rooted in research paid for by the public.

scenes.title: Socialized Loss
scenes.narration_text: Industry patents the winners. The public pays again through high drug prices. When research leads to a dead end, the public eats the loss.
scenes.context: The public bears the financial risk of research failures while private companies keep the profits.

scenes.title: NIH Mission
scenes.narration_text:
You pay for the lottery ticket. They cash the winnings.

The only things the N.I.H. *should* fund are things private companies *cannot* profitably fund:
scenes.context: Identifying what the NIH should focus on: areas where private industry has no financial incentive.

scenes.title: Pragmatic Platforms
scenes.narration_text: Open pragmatic trial platforms: thirty times cheaper than traditional trials, yet receive minimal N.I.H. funding.
scenes.context: Open trial platforms are significantly cheaper and more effective but remain underfunded.

scenes.title: Profitless Generics
scenes.narration_text: Re-purposing generic drugs: more than four thousand seven hundred clinically-tested compounds where no patent equals no profit equals no interest.
scenes.context: The industry's lack of interest in repurposing drugs that are no longer under patent protection.

scenes.title: Comparative Data
scenes.narration_text: Comparative effectiveness data: Head-to-head trials revealing which drugs actually work best (pharma's nightmare).
scenes.context: The need for trials that directly compare the effectiveness of different medications.

scenes.title: Avoiding Competition
scenes.narration_text: These are the *only* things the N.I.H. should be funding. Instead, the N.I.H. explicitly avoids them to "not crowd out industry."
scenes.context: The NIH's policy of avoiding research that might interfere with private industry profits.

scenes.title: Lowering Prices
scenes.narration_text: Translation: "We won't run the trials that would lower drug prices, because the people who set drug prices asked us nicely.".
scenes.context: Criticizing the NIH's refusal to perform research that could lead to lower drug costs.

scenes.title: Outcome Disconnect
scenes.narration_text: The Patient Disconnect: Zero Correlation with Health Outcomes.
scenes.context: Summarizing the lack of alignment between NIH research and actual patient health.

scenes.title: Funding Burden
scenes.narration_text: Correlation between N.I.H. funding priorities and actual disease burden: zero point zero seven.
scenes.context: Final statistic showing near-zero correlation between funding and the actual impact of diseases.

scenes.title: Coin Flip Science
scenes.narration_text: That is not a typo. On a scale of zero (random) to one (perfect), the N.I.H. scores "basically a coin flip."
scenes.context: The author critiques the N.I.H. research funding allocation, comparing its effectiveness to a coin toss.

scenes.title: Patient Desires
scenes.narration_text:
A dartboard would allocate research funding more rationally.

What patients want.

Medicine that works.
scenes.context: Contrasting the irrationality of current funding with the fundamental needs of patients.

scenes.narration_text:

Trials they can join.

A cure before they die.

scenes.narration_text:
Molecular mechanisms.

Papers in prestigious journals.

Research empires.

Institutional overhead.
scenes.context: Describing the academic and bureaucratic outcomes that the N.I.H. prioritizes over cures.

scenes.narration_text: Patients don't control the money. Committees do. And committees optimize for the continued existence of committees.
scenes.context: Explaining how the structure of funding bodies leads to institutional self-preservation.

scenes.narration_text: This is true of all committees, everywhere, since the invention of committees. Nobody has ever convened a committee

that recommended fewer committees.

scenes.narration_text:
one trillion dollars (inflation-adjusted). Diseases eradicated: Zero.

This isn't because eradicating disease is

scenes.narration_text:
impossible:

The W.H.O. eradicated smallpox for three hundred million dollars.

Jonas Salk developed the polio

scenes.context: Laying out the first step of a new research model: incentivizing results rather than processes.

scenes.narration_text:
two. Publish everything: Including failures (especially failures).

three. Eliminate gatekeepers: Let patients

scenes.narration_text:
vote with participation.

four. Automate administration: Smart contracts instead of committees (committees cannot be trusted; see above).
scenes.context: Concluding with the idea of replacing fallible human committees with automated, transparent systems.
